"THE greatest gift that life can give is living," said DR. Harvey W. Wiley when I asked him, ungrammatically but expressively, what he had got out of life.

"Just living is the greatest thing in the world. I have lived fully, so the world owes me nothing, I owe the world everything," said the Rudy giant who can look back over 81 years in which he has been farmer, physician, scientist, teacher and author.

Not that DR. Wiley does much look backward. He is full of ideas and plans for the future, and thoughts of death do not occupy any place in that future.

"I think the reason people fear to die is wholly selfish," he said. "Why seek to destroy the plan of nature? Death is just as much biological matter as birth. One could not exist without the other. I am entirely resigned, therefore, to work out the plan of nature, but I object to doing so any sooner than is quite necessary. I am not sitting down and moping over methods of postponing my funeral. I am just forgetting it."

"To keep young, increase your activities," is his prescription.

Born on the Farm.
He has been incredibly busy all his life. Born on an Indiana farm, he started in with chores as soon as he could toddle. His schooling was sketchy in boyhood for the little one-room Hoosier schoolhouse was miles away from his home, and three months was the usual length of a term. Fortunately, he had access to a peripatetic library belonging to the State which circulated among the various towns. When he was 10 he reached the point when he had to decide on career. Should he be farmer or a professional man?

"I always wanted to be a physician. There were many physicians in my family. My elder sister Elizabeth perhaps influenced me, too, for she wanted to be a physician. She was the first woman who ever applied for admission to Ann Arbor Medical School. She was denied on account of her sex, which impressed my young mind, even then, with a resentment of sex discriminations which made me one of the male 'suffragettes' while women were fighting for the vote many years later. It was a satisfaction to me that Elizabeth did finally become a physician."

"Raised as I was in the narrow life of the country, I had no idea of economic equality as between woman and man, but had no doubt of their mental and moral equality—or even superiority. The women of my own family were most splendid, thoughtful women. I'D in the conviction, quite unconscious, that women were people, homo sapiens. My experience in life has confirmed me in the suspicion that perhaps they are more sapiens than men."

"I have not changed in my view of their economic inferiority. I do not mean by that that there is any inherent reason why women should not be capable as men in economic fields. But they lack experience. I am speaking of women in the mass, of course. There are shining examples of women in economic fields."

Woman's Greatest Work.

"For the most part, however, I have always believed and still do believe, that woman's greatest accomplishment is motherhood. Woman's place is in the home. Not because she cannot get out and beat us men at our own game, but because we can't beat her at hers. I don't mean that women have to be uneducated household drudges. My own wife is a club woman, civic worker, an admirable wife, mother and homemaker. She was one of the original suffragettes! I don't believe any woman has to actually stay at home and cook the oatmeal to be a mother. But to make a home is a full-time job and the higher the grade of the woman the better homemaker she is."

ROOSEVELT FIELD, N. Y.—Feb. 11.
An absent minded motorist today foiled the take-off of the monoplane Columbia—attempt—capture the world's duration flight record. The flight now is scheduled for tomorrow, weather permitting.

Just as Charles Levine, with his pilot, Wilmer Stultz, sped down the runway in an attempt to take off with their heavily loaded plane, motorist drove directly in their path. Stultz quickly veered the plane sharply, bringing it to a halt with dislodged tail skid and a broken rudder post.

Levine, who has had his trans-Atlantic plane groomed for flights of uncertain nature for several days, announced when he arrived at the field that his slight acquaintance with Miss Mabel Bell as passenger would be abandoned for the time being.

It was with the Columbia that Clarence Chamberlin and Bert Acosta made an endurance record last summer, since broken in Germany.
